turns.question: Why is there a big drop in pH on Sept 26?
turns.answer:
Here's what the data shows for the Algalita Pod (Los Alamitos Bay) around Sept 26 — and a caveat up front: the sensors can show you *what* happened, but not *why*.

**What happened (Sept 22–30 window):**
- Through Sept 25, pH sat steady around 7.40–7.50 【T1】.
- Late on Sept 25 local time, pH jumped suddenly — from 8.12 to 11.83 in 30 minutes (01:56 UTC Sept 26) — and climbed to a peak of 12.91, holding between roughly 11.5 and 12.9 for about 15 hours 【T1】.
- Then came the drop you're seeing: 6.36 at 17:56 UTC Sept 26 (from 11.21 half an hour earlier), down to 2.73 early on Sept 27, bottoming near 3.42 on Sept 28, before climbing back to ~7.4 by Sept 30 【T1】【T2】.

**How the system flagged it:** pH was out of range against the operator's configured limits of 6–10 — high (up to 11.92) from 11:26–17:26 UTC on Sept 26, then low (down to 3.418) from 01:56 UTC Sept 27 through Sept 30. It also logged 31 unusual readings, including sudden jumps and values the system describes as "outside the range natural water spans" 【T1】. All of those flags have since cleared.

**What the other sensors did at the same time: nothing matching.** Dissolved oxygen stayed around 8–10 mg/L, ORP around 220–240 mV, conductivity around 58,000–71,000 µS/cm, and temperature followed its normal daily cycle — all in range throughout 【T2】.

**Why it happened:** I can't tell you from this data — no tool here measures a cause, and no other parameter moved with it. As general background only (this pod is in salt water, so don't read it as a limit for this site), the USGS notes that "River waters not affected by contamination generally have a pH in the range of 6.5 to 8.5" 【3】 — both the ~12.9 peak and the ~2.3–3.4 trough are far outside that. These readings passed the device's fault checks, so they stand as measurements; a calibration check on the pH probe would confirm them.

Two data notes: a single pH reading of exactly 0 (the probe's rail value) at 22:00 UTC Sept 24 was excluded as a probable sensor fault — it predates this event and isn't part of it 【T1】. Separately, turbidity readings in this period were stuck at one value and were excluded as a likely failed sensor, so the pod's turbidity channel is worth inspecting 【T2】.

Data covered in this reply: Algalita Pod, 2026-09-22 00:00 to 2026-10-01 00:00 UTC (324 readings); Algalita Pod, 2026-09-26 00:00 to 2026-10-01 00:00 UTC (239 readings).

turns.question: Why is there a big drop in pH on Sept 26?
turns.answer:
Looking at Sept 24–28 for the Algalita Pod (Los Alamitos Bay), the data shows something more complicated than a single drop — pH spiked first, then crashed twice. Times below are local solar time.

**What the pH actually did**
- Through Sept 25 midday it sat around 7.4–7.5.
- On the evening of Sept 25 (~18:00) it jumped: 8.12 at 18:02, then 11.83 thirty minutes later, climbing to a peak of 12.91 around 22:00–00:00. It held roughly 11.5–12.9 overnight.
- The big drop you're seeing came mid-morning Sept 26: from 11.21 at 09:26 to 6.36 at 09:56 — nearly 5 units in half an hour. It then sat around 6.5–7.5 through the afternoon.
- A second crash came late that afternoon: 7.19 at 16:56, then 2.73 at 17:02. It stayed low through Sept 27–28, bottoming at 3.42, before the flags cleared.

Against this pod's configured pH threshold of 6–10, the high stretch on Sept 26 (up to 11.92) and the low stretch from Sept 27–28 (down to 3.42) were both flagged; nothing is flagged now.

**What the other sensors did at the same time**
- Conductivity rose and fell roughly in step: ~59,400 → ~70,900 → ~58,400 µS/cm across the same hours.
- Temperature moved the opposite way: ~84°F down to ~67°F overnight, then back to ~85°F by Sept 26 midday.
- Dissolved oxygen (~7.9–10.2 mg/L) and ORP (~219–241 mV) stayed steady and in range.
- Turbidity can't help here: every reading in this stretch was stuck at one value (Sept 23–Oct 3), a likely failed sensor, so they were excluded and the sensor should be inspected. (Turbidity is a provisional, uncalibrated index in any case, not a calibrated measurement.)

**Why it happened** — the sensor data can't establish a cause. The device's fault checks did not flag these pH readings, but the system marks 30 of them as very unusual, including values "outside the range natural water spans" 【T1】. For background, uncontaminated river waters generally "have a pH in the range of 6.5 to 8.5" 【3†"have a pH in the range of 6.5 to 8.5"】, and "Because pH is based on a logarithmic scale" 【3†"Because pH is based on a logarithmic scale"】, a swing from ~12.9 down to ~2.7 is an enormous change. A calibration check would confirm whether the readings reflect the water.

One housekeeping note: a single pH reading of exactly 0 (the probe's rail) on Sept 24 was excluded as implausible, so it isn't part of these numbers.

turns.question: Why is there a big drop in pH on Sept 26?
turns.answer:
Short answer: the sensor data shows **what** happened, but it can't establish **why**. And what happened around Sept 26 was actually a spike first, then the drop. Here's the shape of it (times in bay-local time, UTC in parentheses):

- **Through Sept 25**, pH sat steady around 7.4–7.5.
- **~6 pm Sept 25** (01:56 UTC Sept 26), it jumped from 8.12 to 11.83 in 30 minutes and kept climbing to a peak of 12.91, then held roughly 11.5–12.9 for about 14 hours 【T1】.
- **~10 am Sept 26** (17:56 UTC), it fell just as fast — 11.21 down to 6.36 in half an hour — and settled back near 7 through the afternoon 【T2】.
- **~5 pm Sept 26** (00:56 UTC Sept 27), it crashed again: 7.19 to 2.73 in 30 minutes. Over Sept 27–28 it sank as low as 3.418 (with a brief dip to 2.3–2.5 the tool flags as very unusual), then recovered gradually, climbing back above 6 by the end of Sept 29 【T1】【T3】.

On the "why": the tool flags the extremes (12.2–12.9, 2.73, 2.3) as outside the range natural water spans, and the documents describe uncontaminated river water as generally pH 6.5–8.5 【2】 — general background, not this pod's limit. Normal day-to-day pH movement in the documents is tied to photosynthesis, respiration and temperature; this event was far larger than that kind of wobble. What the other sensors show: during the high-pH stretch, conductivity rose in step (from ~59,400 up to ~70,900 µS/cm) and temperature dipped (from ~84 to ~67.5 °F), while dissolved oxygen and ORP stayed steady; during the low crash, everything else looked like an ordinary day 【T3】. Nothing in this data measures what drove the swing — a calibration check would confirm whether the readings reflect the water.

Against the operator's configured pH limits of 6–10, the stretch was flagged high on Sept 26 (peak 11.92) and low from Sept 27 through Sept 29; both flags have since cleared, and the pattern wasn't persistent 【T1】【T3】.

Two side notes: one pH reading on Sept 24 (a 0 at the probe's rail) was excluded as a probe fault, before this event; and the turbidity sensor's readings were stuck from Sept 23 to Oct 3 — a likely failed sensor, excluded from the stats, worth inspecting 【T1】【T3】.
